arbh.front: Who narrates the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people” (Arbaʿīn 8)?

arbh.text: Why Arbaʿīn 8 matters: it gives {{c1::the purpose of jihad}}; it stresses {{c2::faith coupled with action}}; it underlines {{c3::the protection of life and wealth}}; and it leaves {{c4::judging the heart to Allah}}

arbh.front: According to the notes on the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people”, what is the primary purpose of jihad in Islam?
arbh.back: To elevate the word of Allah and establish His rule, so that there is justice in the world

arbh.front: In the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people” (Arbaʿīn 8), until when has the Prophet ﷺ been commanded to fight them?
arbh.back: Until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh — that is, until they enter the fold of Islam
arbh.source: Arbaʿīn Ḥadīth 8 — the text in translation

arbh.front: In the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people”, what do people gain once they enter Islam, and what can take it away?
arbh.back: Their lives and property become protected and sacred, “except by the right of Islam”: something like murder or unjust rebellion removes that sanctity

arbh.front: How does the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people” end, and what does it teach about the heart?
arbh.back: “And their reckoning is with Allah.” What is inside a person's heart is between them and Allah; we can only judge what is outward.

arbh.front: According to the notes on the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people”, what does testifying alone give a person, and what must go with it?
arbh.back: The rights and responsibilities of a Muslim — but faith must be coupled with action

arbh.front: How does the Qurʾān mention īmān, as the notes on Arbaʿīn 8 point out?
arbh.back: Again and again together with action, as in <bdi>الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ</bdi>, “those who believe and do righteous deeds”

arbh.front: In the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people”, who are “the people”, according to the vast majority of ḥadīth scholars?
arbh.back: The polytheists of that time: the sworn, open enemies and persecutors of the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims

arbh.front: Why is the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people” not a licence to force people into Islam?
arbh.back: We never judge by one ḥadīth: we read it with the whole ḥadīth corpus and the Qurʾān, and forcing people into Islam contradicts the Qurʾān — <bdi>لَا إِكْرَاهَ فِي الدِّينِ</bdi>, “there is no compulsion in religion” (2:256)

arbh.front: How has the dīn been passed on, according to the notes on Arbaʿīn 8, and what are books for?
arbh.back: By teachers teaching the books, never by books alone. Books are tools of preservation.

arbh.front: Whose life and property are sacred, according to the notes on Arbaʿīn 8?
arbh.back: Everyone's: none may be taken unjustly — though the Muslim's sanctity is of a higher degree

arbh.front: What do the notes on Arbaʿīn 8 say of the claim that Islam spread “by the sword”?
arbh.back: It's debunked. The tradition always knew it was false, and modern researchers now agree: forced conversions, where they happened, were rare and directly against Islamic teachings.

arbh.front: What are the <bdi>مَقَاصِد الشَّرِيعَة</bdi> for, as a whole?
arbh.back: To establish peace, prosperity and security in a healthy society based on morality

arbh.text: The five <bdi>مَقَاصِد الشَّرِيعَة</bdi>, the protection of: {{c1::<bdi>الدِّين</bdi> (faith)}}, {{c2::<bdi>النَّفْس</bdi> (life)}}, {{c3::<bdi>النَّسْل</bdi> (lineage)}}, {{c4::<bdi>العَقْل</bdi> (intellect)}} and {{c5::<bdi>المَال</bdi> (property)}}
arbh.extra: Each is “the protection of” — <bdi>حِفْظ</bdi> — the thing named.
